segments.text: Conservation Amendment Bill. We have our first submitter
today, Federated Farmers. Welcome to the committee this
morning. Take your submission as read, but you've got 15 minutes
with us, so we'll hand it over to you to open up, and then we'll open
up to the committee for questions. So over to you.
Yeah, thank you. So look, we'll just give a bit of a summary for four or five
minutes and then go on to questions.
So yeah, thank you for the opportunity to speak today.
So I'm Richard Dawkins, the Crown Land spokesperson for
Federated Farmers. With me today is Simon Cameron, he's our
Meat and Wool vice chair and West Coast provincial president,
and Mitch Newcombe, our policy lead.
Look, we recognize that this bill has attracted significant
opposition.
Federated Farmers takes a different view.
We support its overall direction because we see a real
opportunity to improve conservation outcomes, while
making public conservation land more practical, responsive,
and effective to manage.
There is a lot in the bill that is practical and overdue.
We support faster and more certain concession processing,
statutory decision-making time frames, and longer concession
terms. We also specifically support proposed Section
6E
, which requires DOC to recognize the economic opportunities
arising from the use and development of conservation land and
resources. We do not see economic activity
and conservation as inherently competing objectives.
Where economic use is compatible with the conservation values of the
land, or contributes to maintaining those values,
it should be able to form part of the management approach.
Active management and farming are really good examples of that kind of
pragmatic economic use.
Grazing can provide an economic return while also contributing
to weed control, reduced fuel loads,
access, pest management,
and the ongoing stewardship of landscapes.
It is therefore a shame that grazing has been progressively
removed, with grazing concessions falling
38% in the past 20 years,
and that leads to our central proposition.
Conservation should be judged by the environmental outcomes it delivers,
not by whether management is active or passive.
For too long, there has been an assumption that removing productive management from
a landscape is inherently better for conservation.
Sometimes that will absolutely be the right answer, but there are large parts of
the conservation estate that are modified landscapes and that have
been managed for generations.
In those places, taking people and stock out does not remove the
need for management.
When grazing, weed control, pest management, and wildfire
mitigation disappear, there can be consequences.
We've seen the spread of wilding pines, we've seen woody weeds establish,
pest numbers rise, access deteriorates,
and fuel loads build.
That is why new area plans should explicitly recognize the
consequences of both intervention and
non-intervention. They should consider active management,
including grazing where appropriate, alongside weed and pest control,
wilding management, wildfire risk, and the impacts on adjoining
landowners.
Planning documents should set the conservation outcomes we are trying to achieve
rather than predetermining which
management philosophy is acceptable.
Our written submission provides practical examples of those pressures.
That is why the bill itself should explicitly recognize active land management,
including grazing, as a legitimate contributor to conservation outcomes.
Look, the other major area for us is around concessions.
We support removing mandatory public notification for routine grazing
license applications, and strongly support statutory
decision-making time frames. Look, we've heard from members that these
applications and renewals, they can take years at a
time. We also support terms of up to 30 years,
and simpler transfer and succession arrangements.
If somebody is investing in fencing, biodiversity, erosion
control, and wildfire mitigation, the tenure should reflect
that kind of investment.
Long-term stewardship should count for something.
Where an allocation process is triggered, demonstrated environmental
performance, infrastructure investment, and local knowledge
should carry real weight.
We also ask the committee to constrain cost recovery.
Reasonable administrative costs are fair, but costs should be
transparent, proportionate, and directly
attributable to the concession activity.
DOC is responsible for more than eight million hectares of public conservation
land. It simply cannot manage every weed, pest, wilding
conifer, fire risk, fence, and access
track across an estate of that scale by itself.
If we accept that conservation is fundamentally an active management
challenge, the question then becomes: who is best
placed to undertake that land management?
Farmers, concessionaires, and neighboring landowners already bring
people, equipment, infrastructure, and generations of local
knowledge.
Parliament should make it easier for that capability to contribute
to conservation.
Sometimes the best outcome will be leaving land alone,
and sometimes it will require active intervention, and sometimes that will
involve grazing. Our request is that Parliament gets the
architecture of the Act right so that the national direction which
follows has the mandate and flexibility to deliver better
conservation outcomes on the ground.
Thank you.
Brilliant. Thank you very much for that submission.
Look, we've got a flurry of questions, so we'll start with Rachel Brooken.
Thank you. So very clear there about the
economic activity. And I think what you're saying,
though, and correct me if I'm wrong, Richard, is that
the type of economic activity that you've been talking to us about is one that
leads to active land management, and I
presume is in the constraints of the examples you gave, such as sheep
grazing and weed maintenance and
fire control.
So my first question is: is that accurate?
Those are the sorts of activities that you're thinking of.
And why I ask that is because the economic development at the moment
is unbounded and could include mining, could include
a whole lot of activities that might not go well
with farming next door.
Yeah. So a lot of those things go hand in hand.
And when a farmer is managing the land, the
weed and pest control is just part of everyday operations, and
Simon Cameron can probably talk to specific examples of that and
just what that farming investment actually involves.
But is that the sort...
Because at the moment, and my question really is the term is very
undefined at the moment.
Yeah, so we're referring to the likes of grazing.
Right.
That's what our reference is. We're not referring to other industries.
So you wouldn't want mining next door?
Well, that's not our remit to comment on, I wouldn't assume.
Well, at a high level, I would say absolutely we are appropriate, but with the
conservation outcomes, certainly-
Thank you
... as part of the decision-making process.
Thank you. Grant.
Yeah. I'm just curious the--
thanks for coming in, team. You've come a long way, Simon, from down the bottom of
the West Coast. The
public notification of
concessions. Explain to me why you're opposed to that.
At the moment, grazing licenses, you can have a grazing
license unnotified with a maximum term of 10 years.
Mm-hmm.
And you don't get a lot of certainty out of that.
A grazing license doesn't come with right of renewals or...
Yeah.
Families have farmed these parcels of land for over 150 years.
Mm-hmm.
And the uncertainty is minimized right down to 10 years.
How can you invest significant amount of
money to maintain that significant area?
And the key point of that is that in a lot of these areas that have been managed
and looked after by farmers for over 150 years, the conservation values,
if any, if they are present, it is largely because of their stewardship that
they are present. Not in spite of grazing, it's because of grazing and the active
land management. So public notification, the problem with it, if you go to,
we've seen it,
guys have gone, "Right, we want the maximum term," so they go up to 15 years as
your maximum. And you get slaughtered at public notification
by Federated Mountain Climbers, Forest and Bird, and the
likes. It's thousands and thousands of signatures from people
in Wellington and Auckland who have never been to where we live.
And these families have looked after these parcels of land for over 150 years.
Mm-hmm.
That's why we don't like public notification. It's not a fair process.
And just a quick sup on all that. And I don't know if you highlighted here the
importance of longer term grazing licenses.
I did mention, yeah.
You're talking 30 years is sort of what you-
We see 30 years as fair. Matt, I don't think that's unreasonable.
No.
It matches a mortgage. With 30 years, it gives you certainty.
You can invest, you can continue to do
more weed and pest control if there is any to be done.
And I say that because there's parcels of land there that we view,
that we obviously want to see grazing return to.
Because through tenure review, we've retired 1.2 million hectares
of New Zealand that now sits in the DOC estate.
It's an extra cost burden to the department.
If we take grazing back to these parcels of land, and you give grazing
concessions for 30 years, there's a significant amount of time where you can
actually invest with confidence that you can actually get a return on your
investment and enhance the
The conservation values that are there.
Mm. Just a quick sup on the grazing, just while we're at this part.
You've given a graph in your submission and shown that from 2006 there
were 754 grazing concessions, and that's now reduced to
Correct.
Or 67. And so that reduction, though, are you putting that
down to it being more restrictive in terms of-
Very restrictive
... access and it becoming progressively harder
over that time?
There's no restriction on public access on these parcels of land.
There's no restriction on public access.
But the department is becoming more and more restrictive of grazing, and any
opportunity that they can retire a grazing license, they absolutely
do, and they'll use any reason to do so.
Well, and the great irony is often that reason is because they're saying, "Hey,
look, this is a pristine environment. There's rare species there.
We need to protect it." Just recently, we've seen one parcel
retired that's actually been actively managed, been farmed for
160 years. So-
Mm
... something changes. Someone comes along and does an inspection and says,
"Look at this fantastic environment."
Mm.
But again, that is because of the farming and the stewardship,
not in spite of it. So yes, we are seeing a significant decline in
grazing concessions, and often, ironically, it's because of the
fantastic job the farmers have done.
Mm.
Thank you. Priyanka.
Thanks.
My question kind of follows on from Rachel's, and it's to your point, Richard,
you've said that you support Section 6E and the change to purpose.
You've also mentioned in your bill that land management should be judged
by conservation outcomes.
Yeah.
The two don't sit together as the bill is currently drafted.
Others, like the Parliamentary Commission for the Environment, have said that
the wording of the bill that to sort of give primacy to
economic development to the greatest extent practicable-
Yeah
... will mean that there's no hierarchy there.
It means that DOC will have to allow for things like mining, like
what Rachel said,
instead of looking at conservation outcomes as primary purpose.
So the two don't really sit together.
Would you then be supportive, would the fifth then be supportive of that wording
being changed to allow for economic development within the bounds of
conservation, with conservation still being the primary purpose?
Yes, absolutely. With that recognition that the two aren't
always mutually exclusive. And in the terms of grazing,
it can actually be used for positive environmental
outcomes. So it actually ticks both boxes.
In some cases, yes, absolutely, it's mutually exclusive-
Mm
... but we would like to see active management and grazing actually
recognized in the planning documents as an environmental tool.
Thank you. Stuart.
Oh, thank you very much.
Over to you, Stuart.
Thanks, Richard and Simon, good to see you both.
The active management interests me, and particularly around
river management, which has not been actively managed
since the catchment boards were disestablished
30, 40 years ago.
Yeah.
So are you guys in favor of active
management to prevent
loss of land and loss of assets, which would mean
including on DOC land? Because obviously that-
Mm
... the problems are set up at the top of the river as well as
further down.
Yeah.
Yeah, it's all a very similar theme, isn't it?
Just locking up something and leaving it and walking away-
Yeah
... that is not effective management.
And in fact, you've got a live case of river management at the moment, don't you?
Yeah, I do.
Yeah.
Mm.
Got a $27,000 bill from
our friendly council, but anyway, that's another story.
So that's after the fact. If you were able to
spend less but
actively manage the river, you'd prevent those problems occurring.
Yeah, of course.
Absolutely supportive of that. Yeah.
Yeah.
Thank you. Look, we've got time for one last question from Lam.
Well, my question was just about the examples at the back that you gave.
So are these areas in pink, are they completely
unmanaged?
Yeah, they're part of land parcels that retired through
tenure review. So started through the '90s till
recently.
And they've been completely retired.
A lot of those hold firm
purchases, they were brought under the Nature Heritage Fund.
They've been completely retired.
They now sit in a DOC estate, and they are essentially a burden to the taxpayer.
And look, a lot of those, they're modified pastures,
they're farms, and they've just been bought,
destocked, all the infrastructure's taken out and then left.
And-
Mm
... public access has gone through, but the roads are now unmanaged.
Likes of Birchwood, you can struggle to get up there now.
Mm-hmm.
Whereas that used to be a very well-maintained road.
You struggle to get in there. And it's just a continuous cost burden to the
taxpayer. And look at DOC, their budget went from 325 million under the
last national government,
and then through the last labor government it was extended out to 830 million.
And now I think they're somewhere around that $7, $800 million still, but they've
still got their hand out for more because they don't have enough.
And there's 1.2 million hectares of extra land there that they've got to try and
manage.
Thank you. And then further on the concession
aspect. So you talked about 30 years just then, but you had in your submission
60 years-
Yeah
... for longer term concessions.
What is the current-
I think there's a typo
... You talk about 10-year grazing license.
That's what they currently are. Grazing licenses are a maximum of 10 years without
public notification, 15 years with public notification.
I think that's a typo, to be fair.
Okay.
It should be 30 years. Matches a
mortgage. It sits with everything else.
That's fair, but it's enough to give you certainty to invest and
to actually go and
Put a plan in place to actively look after and bring back these parcels of
land that, instead of costing the New Zealand taxpayer, these
parcels of land could be... We can generate jobs, we can
produce for the nation to export to the world, a lot of fine wool
Merino,
prime beef. These are great things that have helped build this country for
centuries now.
Let's get back to it, and it creates a better
environment in these parcels of land. It enhances conservation values.
Mm-hmm.
We're not talking about intensive farming, we're talking about extensive farming,
and
that high country extensive pastoral system that really looks after the
environment. You have to. If you don't look after it, it won't look after you or
your animals, so.
Mm-hmm.
Look, thank you very much for your submission today.
Really valuable discussion and points.
Yeah.
And appreciate all your work on it, and for coming so far to submit to us
today. So thank you very much.
Thank you.
Thanks, team.
No problems. And look, we'd extend the invite at any opportunity.
If you'd like to check out some of this land that was retired and is no longer
managed, it is very hard to find a single parcel that is
in better condition now than when it was farm.
So always happy to show you around.
So appreciate that, and it's good for us to get that practical understanding too,
so thank you.
Thank you.
Thank you very much.
So we now welcome our next submitter,
Transpower New Zealand. Welcome to the
select committee.
Thank you.
We'll just let you get settled there.
Now, welcome. You've got 15 minutes with us this morning, and do
take your submission as read. I know it's a pretty weighty submission with lots
of points in there. So, we'll hand it over to you, though, to walk us through it
and then open up for questions.
Thank you. Kia ora koutou. I'm Matt Fanning, head of land owner relations and
property at Transpower. My colleague here, Joanne Moore, our senior legal
counsel.
Thank you for the opportunity to be heard today.
Transpower will be familiar to the committee, so I won't go into a lot of detail
about who we are and what we do.
Look, electricity demand is forecast to grow by 80% by
2050. We're working to connect significant renewable generation to
the grid and meet increasing demand to electrify NZ and grow our
economy. We have a really busy work program of new build and
major upgrade projects to enable that growth.
We also need to ensure that our existing assets are effectively
maintained. We seek regulatory settings that better
enable the important work we do for the benefit of all Kiwis.
A significant part of the National Grid is located on public conservation land.
You'll see some numbers in our submission there.
It's effectively approximately 5% of our transmission lines
network, so significant. More than 2,000 structures,
towers and poles, more than 900 kilometers of transmission lines,
more than 100 kilometers of fiber cable,
more than 600 kilometers of access tracks and other facilities such as
telecommunication sites.
Right.
So that paints a picture for you.
Most of the assets have been there for many, many decades, and in some cases,
going back more than 100 years.
We may also need to cross public conservation land for new assets.
While we'd seek to avoid public conservation land, that may not be possible
given the extensive coverage of public conservation land across New Zealand.
I believe it's about a third of New Zealand's total land area.
And the long and linear nature of our assets, it's hard to avoid it, even if we
really needed to or wanted to.
Look, we support the bill,
but we seek several changes to ensure the policy intent of the bill is realized,
that being to modernize the concessions application process, standardize
concessions management, and improve the allocation of concessions
opportunities.
There are some key changes that we have sought in our submission.
Jo's going to elaborate on those. But just as a quick summary,
we seek that our high frequency, low impact activities on our
existing assets on public conservation land should be exempted from
requiring a concession.
Second, that some of our more significant upgrade and replacement activities on
those existing assets should have a pre-approved concession
status.
Including the definition of critical infrastructure into the bill that includes the
National Grid,
and excluding that defined critical infrastructure from any
competitive allocation of concessions.
Allowing easements to be granted for a term of 60 years for critical
infrastructure. Not requiring payment for adverse effects from critical
infrastructure,
and requiring DOC to undertake greater consultation with critical infrastructure
operators when developing or amending the NCPS.
And also, so preventing the prohibition or restriction of critical infrastructure
in that National Conservation Policy Statement, NCPS.
Just a little bit about our concessions process currently.
We usually require easement type concessions, given the long linear
nature of our assets and the non-exclusive use,
usually electricity and or telecommunications easements and rights of way for
access.
The current settings in the Conservation Act do not recognize the extent of our
existing assets on public conservation land.
Our prevailing legislation is the Electricity Act, and under that, we have the
authority to enter land to inspect, maintain, and operate our assets
generally, but we seek greater consistency on how those rights apply to public
conservation land under the Conservation Act.
An alternative approach that we haven't called out in our submission would be to
exempt all activities authorized by the Electricity Act from the need to
obtain concessions. Jo, I'll hand it to you.
Okay. Right, so turning to
the exemptions process in the bill, as Matt said, we support that.
We've got significant aged assets throughout the
country on public conservation land, and we think given the
high frequency of that work, it's a known quantity, what we're
doing, what the effects are. We think that an exemption regime should be able to
be developed with conditions.
There are unlikely to be any surprises in terms of what we're doing.
So we think that is doable These maintenance
activities are ongoing. We must do them if the assets are going
to stay operational. And this is particularly given their age, as Matt
said, most of them are
decades old.
And we've sought greater consistency in our submission with the Electricity
Act. Through the Electricity Act, we can carry out inspections and
maintenance activities by giving notice and then working with the relevant
landowners on conditions. So, that's the process we've sought to be embedded in the
Conservation Act.
We've also suggested an approach that would allow urgent works to be
carried out. So the emergency provisions in the Conservation Act
currently, and also the RMA, are really narrow.
They require there to be an imminent threat and given
the scale of our assets, it takes some time to design a solution.
But the works are still just as urgent,
but we just don't replace a wooden pole with a wooden pole because we need to
design the solution. So that means the works are urgent, not
imminent.
We also
note that one reason for wanting this consistency is that if we had
to get concessions for all of our work, things would really come to a halt,
and that would be both probably at our end and at the conservation end.
We're just doing this work all the time on those hundreds and hundreds of
assets that Matt's mentioned.
We also support the pre-approval process.
So what we've done in our submission, we've defined what we think are these
regular routine activities, and then the things that go beyond that scope, we've
put them into the pre-approval category.
So they would be subject to the need to obtain a concession
with conditions set in advance.
And we think that pre-approval pathway would also streamline the concession
process. So as Matt said, we've got quite a lot of work coming up, and
we're keen to make sure that all regulatory processes work as efficiently as
possible.
We've also sought that these exemptions and pre-approvals
for the grid are embedded in the statute rather than being left for subsequent
decision-making at the NCPS level.
You'll be aware that the draft proposed NCPS was
notified, and it had a really, really narrow exemption
regime in there. It applied to, I think, four activities.
So news of the day reporting,
and the collection of air and water for research, and observational
research. So it didn't really align with the policy intent of the bill, which was
to streamline concession process and remove them from many activities, the
everyday activities.
So that's the reason we have sought that specificity in
relation to the grid. We've also sought a definition of critical
infrastructure,
and the reason for that is we think some provisions need to be extended out for
infrastructure.
Like federated farmers, we think concessions should be 60 years for our
infrastructure.
It's long-lived, and a requirement to have a 30-year time limit just means we
will have to come back again. The assets aren't going anywhere.
And so we typically seek that 60-year concession,
60-year limit for our easements around the country.
We have also sought that the provisions in relation to
critical infrastructure are removed from the competitive allocation process for
concessions. We won't be competing with anyone else in relation to concessions
we need for works on the grid.
And we've also sought that when developing the
NCPS, that there's a requirement for DOC to engage with infrastructure
operators.
We know what's there, we know what work we need to do.
It's really important that the NCPS enables our activities.
If there's a gap, for whatever reason, there's a requirement to decline
concessions, and we can't be in that position.
And the final point I wanted to make is, the bill
proposes a broadening of some measures in the Act to enable payments for adverse
effects. And we're concerned that that is veering into
duplication with the RMA and the Wildlife Act.
The Wildlife Act and the RMA already cover
adverse effects and manage the adverse effects of our activities and
get into compensation when required.
So we've suggested that be deleted.
So I'm happy to take questions.
Look, thank you very much. We've got a few questions. We'll go first to Rachel.
Thank you. Thank you for that.
Couple of questions. And I think how
I'm framing your submission is, you've got all these existing assets
on conservation land.
So
you think there should be an easier way through.
Mm.
But then you're also talking about... And most of your submission is on that point.
But then you've also noted that you might want to put your assets on some of that
land. So I've got two different questions-
Mm-hmm
... around those two different points.
In your definition of critical infrastructure,
you just say it includes your stuff.
Would it be easier just to refer to
Transpower explicitly? Because I'm wondering what other critical
infrastructure do you think there might be that is of this linear
nature and goes through so much conservation land?
There may be distribution assets that are in conservation land.
Mm.
Yeah.
And I know that the generators have got some easements as well.
Okay.
So they may, we've sought a 60-year term for our
concessions-
... and the easements that result from it.
Yeah.
That might be appropriate for the generators and others.
So that's the reason we've put includes.
Yeah, no.
Because there may be other parties.
I thought that might be the reason, but-
Yeah
... wanted to just draw that out. And then,
I just wonder, I know
Transpower does a lot of planning.
You invest a lot of time in that for obvious reasons, and you've given us
Appendix B, you've given us an example of the Nelson Marlborough area,
and I see that the lines, they go through quite a lot of conservation
parkland, but they seem to miss the national parks there.
Mm-hmm.
Is that standard? Have you got much infrastructure on national
parks?
We have got some.
In Manapōuri.
Right. That makes sense.
For example-
Yeah
... there's some in national park in the North Island.
I believe there's some Tongariro as well.
Probably going to be out-
Desert Road, you see the lines kind of going down the landscape there.
I, mm, yeah.
There will be some parts, but there's lots of different types of conservation land
and-
Sure
... national parks being the most precious.
Yeah. Well, I was just wondering then, and with your planning for new
infrastructure,
would you anticipate any of that going over national park land?
We would do a route selection process, and we would
identify sensitive environments and do our best to avoid them.
And to the extent that there is a high volume of
conservation estate or public conservation land, you
should expect that the national parks and those other
areas that are the crown jewels would be given a stronger weighting in
terms of avoiding them.
But is there any planning at the moment to do build more new
infrastructure in areas that might be in
public conservation, given that a lot of it is up the spine of the South
Island?
We can't-
There's, we can't say that would never be the case-
No, I'm not asking you that
... but, yeah, but certainly at this stage, I'm not aware of anything.
But as we
go through our planning for new lines and route selection processes-
Yeah
... we have to go through a constraints exercise and identify where those lines
would go, and given there's so much conservation land-
Yeah, and then to Queenstown might be, but yeah, we can't really-
Yeah. Yes. Correct. And there's so much different types of conservation land as
well. National parks are obviously the most-
Yeah
... at one end, but you've got lots of other different types of reserves and that
sort of thing as well. So, I, I-
We do have an example.
Yes.
Currently, which I think we've talked to the-
... select committee previously on other bills-
Yeah
... where we've got some assets that are in a wetland, and they need to
be,
the towers are getting quite old, and so we're proposing to replace them.
But through that, we are working with DOC and others to try and relocate them-
New route
... out of the wetland, but then they would most likely end up in DOC estate.
Yep.
Yeah. But they're currently-
Further out
... they're currently in a-
For a good environmental reason. Yeah
... yeah, so they're currently in a nationally critical DOC-
... managed wetland, and we're trying to get them out of that.
They'll go on, they will stay on DOC land, but they'll be out of the wetland, so
it'll be the better location overall. Yeah.
That would trigger an easement.
Interesting example. Grant?
Yeah. Look, I'm just pushing actually, as a landowner with one single
tower sitting on our property. We
have that process as a private landowner, they get in contact, blah, blah, blah,
blah, blah. How does that differ to what you do with DOC?
Because I know how it operates from my perspective.
I literally get the, they just, they tell me when they're coming. Is it okay?
"Sure, go ahead. No issues." Yeah.
Yeah. I can answer that. We notify DOC in the same way we do any other
landowner. It's usually at the local kind of ranger level.
We work with them on a day-to-day basis, making sure that they've got notice and
that we're complying with their requirements.
So, where does the concession part come in for the actual activities?
I suppose is the question I'm asking.
Yeah.
Yeah. So that's a really complicated question in terms of the alignment
between the Electricity Act and the Conservation Act, because the two don't sit
nicely together. So, our answer would be that the Electricity Act provides the
notice, and then we work with DOC as per usual, because both of them are
property regime.
Mm.
But what we're trying to do here is avoid any question about how those two
pieces of legislation work together and make them consistent.
Thank you. Lan.
Thank you so much for such a clear submission.
I just was interested about with the NCPS,
like potentially exceeded. You mention in your
sort of criteria where it could specify, for example, tree
trimming and removal undertaken by qualified arborists, a suitably
qualified and experienced ecologist to monitor vegetation removal,
is generally, like when you're referring to that, it's
contractors coming in, they're clearing the areas directly
around the infrastructure. Like that kind of thing?
Mm-hmm. That's right.
Yeah.
I mean, it seems very-
Thank you.
Thank you.
We'll take one last quick question from Priyanka.
Thanks. Actually similar to Grant.
So I was trying to get a sense of how onerous the current state of play is to
get concessions from DOC, or whether it's just you're trying to
sort of align the two pieces of legislation to avoid any doubt.
Is it?
I think it would, well, from our perspective, I think it's the latter.
We're trying to align the two.
